title: Plant hazards, allergens and hazardous contamination
audience: Garden clean-up workers and crew leaders who handle plants, hedges, leaf litter and garden debris and who may encounter animal or unknown contamination on site.
learningOutcomes: Identify plants and plant materials that commonly cause skin, eye, respiratory or allergic reactions.
Recognise suspicious sap, thorns, needles, animal droppings and other contamination without touching or smelling them.
Apply the control steps for plant hazards, including the use of gloves, eye protection and barriers.
Isolate and refer unidentified or hazardous contamination to the authorised person and record the referral.

instruction.heading: Why plant hazards are easy to underestimate
instruction.body: Plants are part of the job, and their hazards are often treated as minor. Yet many garden plants and their parts irritate skin, cause blistering when the sap meets sunlight, damage the eyes or trigger allergic reactions. Pollen, spores, fine dust from dry leaves and mould in damp mulch can irritate the airways. Thorns and spines cause punctures that can become infected. A worker who knows which plants are common hazards, and who protects against them before the job starts, avoids many of the minor injuries that take a team off the job. This lesson does not replace a full medical or allergy assessment. Anyone with a known allergy or sensitivity should tell the supervisor before the job starts, and the business should record it in the safety plan.

instruction.heading: Plants, sap, thorns and allergens
instruction.body: Begin each job by looking at the plants in the work area. Look for plants with milky or coloured sap, plants with spines or thorns, plants with irritant hairs, and plants with berries or seed pods that may be toxic. Do not identify a plant by touch or smell. Some sap causes a burning rash after exposure to sunlight, and some berries are toxic if eaten. Wear gloves that resist sap and punctures, and eye protection when cutting. Keep tools clean so that sap does not build up on blades and handles. Wash exposed skin with water and soap after the job, and wash contaminated clothing separately. If a worker develops a rash, swelling, breathing difficulty or eye irritation, stop work, move away from the plant, and follow the first-aid and emergency procedure. Severe reactions require urgent medical help.

instruction.heading: Suspicious contamination and unknown material
instruction.body: Sometimes the hazard is not the plant but what is with it. Animal droppings, unknown liquids, needles, syringes, stained soil, dead animals, unusual residues and containers with no label can all appear in a garden. Do not touch, smell or move these items with bare hands. Stop work in the area, keep others back and place barriers or markers where the material is located. Take a photograph from a safe distance with the client's consent, and record the location. Do not attempt to clean, spray, bag or dispose of the material unless the business's procedure and the applicable licence or authority allow it for that exact material. Regulated biological or chemical contamination must be handled by authorised personnel only. Do not use a pesticide or cleaning product to treat the material, and do not improvise a disposal method. Inform the supervisor and the client, and follow the escalation route.

instruction.heading: Protecting people while work continues
instruction.body: When a hazard has been isolated, the rest of the work can often continue. Set a barrier around the hazard, move the team away from it and check that the barrier holds. Do not work on the rest of the garden in a way that moves the contamination, for example by using a blower across the hazard area. If the hazard is in a hedge or dense growth, cut the vegetation around it and leave the hazard in place for the authorised person. Do not allow children, pets or neighbours into the marked area. Record the hazard, the barrier, the time and the person informed. Stop the work if the barrier cannot be maintained or if the hazard spreads.

instruction.heading: Verification and referral
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the hazard decision rather than the paperwork. A competent worker can name the plant hazards on a job, describe the controls they chose, explain why they did not touch an unknown material and identify the authorised person to call. Escalate to the supervisor for any unknown material, any suspected biological or chemical contamination, any exposure, any reaction or injury, and any situation where the hazard cannot be contained. Do not certify that an area is clean or safe. Record only what has been observed and what has been done.

procedure: Before starting, check the client's notes for allergies, sensitivities and known plant hazards, and tell the team.
Survey the work area for suspect plants, sap, thorns, droppings, needles, containers and unknown material, looking before reaching.
Put on gloves and eye protection suitable for the plants and the task before cutting or clearing.
Do not identify any plant or material by touch or smell. Keep clear of any unknown material.
If unknown or suspicious material is found, stop work in the area, keep others back and mark a barrier.
Take photographs from a safe distance with consent and record the location, the time and the people nearby.
Refer the material to the supervisor and, where needed, to the authorised person. Do not clean, spray or bag it yourself.
After the job, wash exposed skin and separate contaminated clothing. Record any reaction and the first-aid response.

workedExamples.situation: A worker finds a sap-filled stem and some unidentified animal droppings near the base of a hedge that must be trimmed for the client.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What controls do you apply, and what do you not do?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not touch the sap or the droppings and do not smell them. Mark the area and keep the team back. Protect the crew with gloves and eye protection for the trimming, and trim the hedge on the side away from the marked area if the job allows. Do not spray the material or bag it. Photograph it from a distance with consent, inform the supervisor and the client, and record the referral to the authorised person.

workedExamples.situation: A crew member clearing leaves has a red, itchy rash on the forearm after handling a plant with milky sap, and they are now shaking the arm and having difficulty breathing.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first action, and what should be recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: Breathing difficulty is a sign of a severe reaction and needs urgent help, so call emergency services immediately and follow the emergency procedure. Move the worker away from the plant and remove any contaminated gloves. Do not wait to see if it settles. Record the plant, the exposure, the first-aid response and the time, and inform the supervisor.

equipmentAndPpe: Chemical-resistant or sap-resistant gloves suitable for plant handling
Long sleeves and long trousers for thorny or sap-bearing plants
Dust mask or respirator where dry leaf litter or mould is disturbed, selected for the hazard
Barrier tape, cones or markers for isolated hazards
Water, soap and a clean-up kit for skin exposure
Camera or phone for recording at a safe distance, with consent

commonErrors.error: Touching or smelling an unknown plant or material to find out what it is.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not touch or smell. Isolate the material, record it and refer it for identification or authorised handling.

commonErrors.error: Using a blower across an isolated contamination area, which spreads the material.
commonErrors.prevention: Use hand tools only in the work zone, and keep blowers and sprays away from the marked hazard.

commonErrors.error: Spraying a product on an unknown material because it seems the quickest option.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not treat unknown material. Refer it to the authorised person, and use only products that the business is licensed or authorised to use.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring a mild rash or irritation because it seems minor.
commonErrors.prevention: Report every reaction. Follow the first-aid procedure and seek medical advice when symptoms persist or worsen.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Biological and chemical contamination can be regulated, and its handling, transport and disposal may require licensed or authorised personnel. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to handle or treat regulated contamination.

Using a pesticide or other product on plants or contamination may need a licence or specific authority. In New South Wales, the EPA's 2018 fact sheet says people who spray weeds for payment need a ground-applicator licence, and the requirement has applied since 1 July 2018. This lesson does not grant that licence.

The model WHS framework requires duty holders to manage biological hazards from the work environment to the level that is reasonably practicable, and to rank controls for certain risks, moving from the most reliable option downward.

qualityStandard: Client allergy and sensitivity information has been checked and communicated before the job starts.
No unknown plant or material has been touched, smelled, sprayed or bagged by the crew.
Any suspected contamination is isolated with a barrier and referred to the authorised person, with the referral recorded.
Each reaction, exposure or injury has been treated under the first-aid procedure and recorded.
documentationEvidence: Pre-job hazard check record, including client allergy information.
Contamination or unknown-material referral with the location, time, photographs taken at a safe distance and the person informed.
Injury or exposure record, including the plant involved and the first-aid response.
Record of barriers placed and removed, and of the authorised person's attendance.
summary: Plants cause irritation, allergy, sun-triggered sap reactions and punctures. Protect against them before cutting.
Do not touch, smell or move unknown material. Isolate it and refer it.
Do not treat, spray or bag unknown contamination without authority.
Report every reaction, and treat severe reactions as emergencies.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker finds an unlabelled container with a liquid in a garden bed. What is the correct first action?
options: Open it carefully and smell it to find out what it is, since most liquids in a garden bed are harmless.
Stop, keep others back, do not touch or smell it, mark the area and refer it to the supervisor.
Pour the liquid onto the mulch so it is out of the way and the crew can continue with the clean-up.

knowledgeChecks.question: A plant on the job has milky sap that causes a burning rash after exposure to sunlight. Which control is most effective?
options: Work in full sun without protection, since the sap only matters when it rains.
Rinse the sap off with a solvent that is kept in the van.
Wear sap-resistant gloves and eye protection, and keep the sap off the skin and tools.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker has difficulty breathing after handling plant material. What is the correct response?
options: Call emergency services immediately and follow the emergency procedure, moving the worker away from the plant.
Wait ten minutes to see if it settles, then continue the work with the plant material as before, since it is usually mild.
Give the worker a drink and ask them to rest in the van for a while before they return to the job site.
